Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Vignette:
# Rajesh

Rajesh was twenty-six when Amar moved in. They had been together for two years, meeting through friends at a cricket match, and Amar had always been attentive in public—bringing him coffee at the shop, remembering his mother's birthday. The first time Amar hit him was over a text message from a colleague. Rajesh had been standing in the kitchen of their apartment in Jackson Heights, and Amar came behind him, grabbed his shoulder hard, and slammed his head against the cabinet door. It happened so fast that Rajesh's mind seemed to lag behind his body's shock. The pain bloomed across his temple. When he turned around, Amar was already crying, saying it would never happen again, that he was stressed about work, that he loved him. Rajesh believed him because he wanted to, because the violence seemed like an aberration, a crack in something otherwise solid.

It was not an aberration. Over the next eight months, there were other incidents—Amar's fist against Rajesh's ribs one night when he came home late from the shop, Amar's hands around his neck during an argument about money, Amar's voice becoming something unrecognizable, animal and full of contempt. Each time, Rajesh found himself frozen, unable to fight back effectively, unable to leave. What frightened him most was not the violence itself but his own paralysis in the face of it. Afterward, alone, he would replay the moments obsessively—the things he could have said, the ways he could have protected himself, the moment he should have pushed back harder. He had come to believe that his failure to stop it, his inability to match Amar's aggression with his own, made him complicit in his own harm. The guilt settled into him like a permanent weight.

The breaking point came when Amar, in a rage about Rajesh spending time with his brother, pinned him against the wall and beat him until Rajesh's vision blurred. When Amar finally released him and left for work, Rajesh sat on the floor of their bathroom and called his sister. She came within the hour and took him to her house. That was three months ago.

Now, at twenty-nine, Rajesh was trying to rebuild. He had ended things with Amar, moved back into an apartment of his own, and returned to running his electronics shop in Flushing. But the trauma had woven itself into the fabric of his daily life in ways he could not seem to untangle. At night, sleep was nearly impossible. He would lie in bed, his body tense, listening for sounds in the hallway, convinced that Amar would find him. His heart would race at the smallest noise—a neighbor's footsteps, a car horn outside. During the day, he felt safer, but the safety was fragile. When customers came into the shop, particularly men who stood too close or spoke in a certain tone, Rajesh's entire nervous system would activate. He found himself scanning their faces, their hands, assessing threat in ordinary transactions. An older man asking about phone cases last week had approached the counter, and the particular way he moved his shoulders triggered something primal in Rajesh—a flash of Amar's body language right before impact.

Worse were the sensory ambushes. A customer would brush past him, and the smell of sweat—not even Amar's particular scent, just the generic human smell of exertion—would send him spiraling. The memory would arrive fully formed and unwelcome: the weight of Amar's body, the smell of his skin, the specific timbre of his voice. These moments came without warning, and with them came a rage that terrified Rajesh. He would excuse himself to the back room, his fists clenched, fury coursing through him with such intensity that he barely recognized himself. The rage was not always attached to a clear image; sometimes it was just the raw emotional residue of the trauma, flooding through him like a physical toxin.

His body had become unreliable to him. His heart would race at unpredictable moments—in the middle of a conversation, while sitting alone in his apartment, during moments that were objectively safe. He had come to distrust his own physical responses, to interpret every flutter of anxiety as evidence that danger was imminent, that his body knew something his rational mind did not. He could not rely on himself to regulate, to calm down, to be present. His sister had noticed his withdrawal; his mother had begun asking pointed questions. He had started calling in sick to the shop more often, unable to face the unpredictability of customer interactions, the weight of being vigilant for eight hours straight.

It was his sister who finally insisted he see someone. She found him a therapist who specialized in trauma, and Rajesh, exhausted by the effort of surviving his own nervous system, agreed. What he fears most now is that the trauma is permanent, that he will never feel safe in his own body again. What he hopes for, though he barely allows himself to articulate it, is that someday he might walk into his shop and simply sell a phone without his entire being braced for attack.
